# Building an Efficient GADDAG in Rust for Scrabble Move Generation

## Overview: GADDAG vs. DAWG in Scrabble AI

Scrabble AI move generation places unique demands on dictionary data structures. A traditional approach uses a **DAWG (Directed Acyclic Word Graph)** – essentially a minimized trie of the lexicon – as described by Appel and Jacobson’s “World’s Fastest Scrabble Program”[\[1\]](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15451-s06/www/lectures/scrabble.pdf#:~:text=ABSTRACT%3A%20An%20efficient%20backtracking%20algorithm,suited%20to%20the%20adversary)[\[2\]](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15451-s06/www/lectures/scrabble.pdf#:~:text=SCRABBLE%20is%20a%20registered%20trademark,any%20strategic%20concepts%2C%20but%20its). However, generating moves with a DAWG can be inefficient when **“hooking”** new words onto existing board letters[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=DAWG,the%20trie%20will%20be%20fruitless). The **GADDAG** (an acronym pun: a DAG prefixed by its own reverse) is a specialized lexicon automaton introduced by Steven Gordon (1994) to speed up move generation by handling hooked letters more directly[\[4\]](https://hana-sebia.github.io/uploads/faster-scrabble-gordon.pdf#:~:text=the%20trie%20of%20a%20large,moves%20more%20than%20twice%20as)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=A%20GADDAG%20is%20a%20data,1). In practice, using a GADDAG yields roughly *twice the move-generation speed* of a DAWG at the cost of about *5× more memory*[\[6\]](https://hana-sebia.github.io/uploads/faster-scrabble-gordon.pdf#:~:text=finite%20automaton%20that%20avoids%20the,by%20the%20decreasing%20cost%20of)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=moves%20require%20words%20that%20,1). Modern Scrabble engines like **Quackle** have adopted GADDAG for its speed[\[8\]](https://people.csail.mit.edu/jasonkb/quackle/doc/how_quackle_plays_scrabble.html#:~:text=This%20block%20takes%20a%20rack,Faster%20Scrabble%20Move%20Generation%20Algorithm).

**DAWG recap:** A DAWG is a compressed trie (prefix tree) that merges suffixes of words to save space[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=A%20GADDAG%20is%20a%20specialization,big%20as%20a%20simple%20DAWG). It excels at prefix queries (e.g. “words starting with QUA”) and quick word validations. Scrabble move generators using DAWGs (e.g. the Maven engine) enumerate moves by *backtracking*: for each anchor point on the board, they recursively build possible left prefixes from rack tiles and then traverse the DAWG forward for the right part of the word[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=DAWG,the%20trie%20will%20be%20fruitless). This backtracking is *non-deterministic* and can waste time exploring prefixes that don’t lead to valid plays[\[10\]](https://hana-sebia.github.io/uploads/faster-scrabble-gordon.pdf#:~:text=finite%20automaton%20that%20avoids%20the,For%20a%20typical%20lexicon%2C%20the)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=It%20fails%2C%20however%2C%20to%20address,the%20trie%20will%20be%20fruitless). For example, to find words that hook onto the letter P in an existing word “HARPY” with two empty spaces before P, a DAWG-based algorithm would need to search for all words of the form \_\_P\_\_\_\_ by traversing many branches of the trie – many of which fail to produce P in that third position[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=DAWG,the%20trie%20will%20be%20fruitless).

**GADDAG approach:** The GADDAG pre-computes partial rotations of each word to eliminate this inefficiency. Every word is stored not only in forward form but in all possible ways it could be split into a prefix and suffix around some letter. Specifically, for each word, every possible prefix is **reversed** and concatenated with the remaining suffix, separated by a special delimiter (often noted as \+ or @)[\[12\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Here%20are%20its%20prefixes%20and,changed%20into%20the%20DAG%20version)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=For%20any%20word%20in%20a,is%20a%20concatenation%20operator). For instance, the word **CARES** yields these GADDAG strings (using \+ as the separator):

* C+ARES (split before the first letter)

* AC+RES (split before second letter)

* RAC+ES (split before third letter)

* ERAC+S (split before fourth letter)

* SERAC+ (split before the last letter)[\[14\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Here%20are%20its%20prefixes%20and,changed%20into%20the%20DAG%20version)[\[15\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=GADDAG.%20We%E2%80%99ll%20find%20,to%20RE%20to%20get%20CARES)

This means the GADDAG contains a deterministic path for **REV(prefix) \+ suffix** of every word[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=For%20any%20word%20in%20a,is%20a%20concatenation%20operator). In the above example, if the board has the substring “RE”, we reverse it to “ER” and search the GADDAG. Finding the entry ERAC+S indicates that **CA** can be placed before “RE” and **S** after to form **CARES**[\[16\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=What%E2%80%99s%20the%20point%20of%20this%3F,to%20RE%20to%20get%20CARES). In effect, *“the GADDAG is really just a DAWG that contains every dictionary word at every possible entry point into that word”*[\[17\]](https://seth.rocks/projects/scrabble/#:~:text=Stated%20another%20way%2C%20the%20GADDAG,while%20matching%20on%20the%20board). The delimiter symbol signals the transition point (the hooked letter) where leftward assembly (prefix) stops and rightward assembly (suffix) begins[\[18\]](https://seth.rocks/projects/scrabble/#:~:text=As%20an%20example%2C%20consider%20a,point%20between%20the%20board%20and)[\[19\]](https://seth.rocks/projects/scrabble/#:~:text=blank%20spot%20on%20the%20board%2C,not%2C%20the%20candidate%20is%20ignored). By traversing, say, the P branch of a GADDAG, one can directly enumerate all words containing P and get the letters before and after P in one go[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=searches%20through%20the%20trie%20will,be%20fruitless). This drastically reduces dead-ends because we no longer guess prefixes – the structure **“avoids the non-deterministic prefix generation”** of DAWG algorithms by encoding those prefix possibilities upfront[\[10\]](https://hana-sebia.github.io/uploads/faster-scrabble-gordon.pdf#:~:text=finite%20automaton%20that%20avoids%20the,For%20a%20typical%20lexicon%2C%20the).

**Memory trade-off:** Storing each word in *N* rotated forms (for word length *N*) obviously enlarges the dataset. On average, a word of length \~5 (older Scrabble lexica) or \~8–10 (modern lexica) is stored that many times[\[21\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Yeah%2C%20it%E2%80%99s%20storing%20a%20lot,have%20is%20closer%20to%2010). A naive pointer-based GADDAG trie can be extremely large (even **\>1 GB** for a few hundred-thousand words)[\[22\]](https://williame.github.io/#:~:text=A%20naive%20sparse%20implementation%20of,well%20worth%20compressing%20your%20GADDAG). However, because many rotations share common tails, there is significant redundancy to exploit. In practice, the GADDAG is stored as a minimized directed acyclic graph (just like a DAWG) to merge identical suffix subtrees[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this)[\[24\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Just%20reading%2Flearning%20about%20GADDAG%20now,in%20a%20DAFSA%20might%20work). Gordon noted that *“there are lots of duplicate nodes, so FSA minimization is very effective”*, reducing the size to roughly 5× a DAWG[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this). Modern implementations report that a full Scrabble GADDAG (≈200k words) can be as little as **4–6 MB** in memory when compressed[\[25\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=With%20modern%20computers%20it%E2%80%99s%20also,regenerate%20it%20on%20the%20client), well within CPU cache levels (for reference, Quackle’s GADDAG easily fits in L3 cache). This is a worthwhile trade-off, as move-generation is often the tight loop in a Scrabble AI[\[26\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=list%20is%205%2C%20but%20that,have%20is%20closer%20to%2010)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=moves%20require%20words%20that%20,1). As one developer quipped, fitting the GADDAG in cache “can mean an order of magnitude speedup” in move generation[\[27\]](https://williame.github.io/#:~:text=want%20to%20get%20the%20memory,well%20worth%20compressing%20your%20GADDAG).

## Rust Implementations and Data Structures

To implement a GADDAG in Rust efficiently, we need to focus on memory layout and graph compression. A straightforward trie with heap-allocated nodes (each containing a HashMap\<char, Node\> or similar) would be too slow and memory-heavy. Instead, consider these strategies and resources:

* **Finite State Automaton (FSA) libraries:** One convenient approach is to leverage Rust’s [fst crate](https://crates.io/crates/fst) (Fast Succinct Trie by Andrew Gallant). The fst crate can build a minimal DFA (determinisic finite automaton) for a set of strings very efficiently. Developer Amédée d'Aboville created an open-source Rust library *fst-gaddag* that uses fst to store GADDAG data compactly[\[29\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=%24%20fst%20set%20,fst)[\[30\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=When%20we%20build%20a%20GADDAG,sorted). The idea is to generate all REV(prefix)+suffix variants for every word and insert them into the FST builder, which will sort them and produce a compressed automaton. In his tests, building a GADDAG FST for \~200k words (NWL18 Scrabble lexicon) took only \~3 seconds and resulted in a \~6 MB automaton file (4 MB gzipped)[\[31\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Scrabble%20AI%2C%20and%20this%20significantly,so%20it%E2%80%99s%20worth%20the%20tradeoff)[\[30\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=When%20we%20build%20a%20GADDAG,sorted). The automaton can be memory-mapped or embedded as a static binary (using include\_bytes\!) for ultra-fast read-only access[\[32\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=static%20dict%3A%20Fst%3A%3ASet%20%3D%20include_bytes%21%28,). Queries like exact lookup, prefix, suffix, or substring search can then be done by leveraging automaton state intersections (the fst crate supports operations like .starts\_with and regex-like concatenation of automatons)[\[33\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Exact%20check)[\[34\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Substring%20Search). For example, to find all words containing “AX” anywhere, one can search the GADDAG FST for keys starting with XA (the reversed substring) and collect matches[\[34\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Substring%20Search). Amédée’s blog post **“The 2 Data Structures you need in a Scrabble AI”** and the accompanying code on GitHub[\[35\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=There%20we%20have%20it%2C%20the,blocks%20for%20a%20Scrabble%20AI) provide a great blueprint for using this method.

* **Custom trie with minimization:** If using an external crate is undesirable (e.g., if you need dynamic insertions or a custom data format), you can build a minimized trie in pure Rust. One technique is to implement a **DAFSA (Deterministic Acyclic Finite State Automaton)** construction: insert all words in sorted order and merge equivalent subtrees on the fly[\[24\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Just%20reading%2Flearning%20about%20GADDAG%20now,in%20a%20DAFSA%20might%20work). This is the classic algorithm for DAWG construction (described by researchers like Daciuk, Mihov, etc., and in \[Steve Hanov’s blog\][\[36\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=stevehanov)). The GADDAG generation can follow the same pattern – generate all rotated forms, sort them, then construct a minimal graph. Developers on a Zig forum discussing GADDAG optimizations noted that sorting plus minimization yields huge memory savings, as expected[\[24\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Just%20reading%2Flearning%20about%20GADDAG%20now,in%20a%20DAFSA%20might%20work)[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this). For instance, Steven Gordon himself commented that his original implementation used a single large array for nodes with 22-bit offsets as pointers and the remaining bits for flags/char data, to avoid pointer overhead[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this). By packing fields into 32-bit or 64-bit integers and using indices instead of references, one can drastically reduce memory footprint and improve cache locality. One programmer reported success using a 32-bit node struct (24 bits for child pointer index, 5 bits for the letter, and 3 bits for flags) – achieving about **40 MB for 360k words uncompressed**, which they planned to further compress by merging duplicate subtrees[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this)[\[37\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=I%20optimized%20the%20gaddag,now%20a%2032%20bits%20node). Another approach is to output the automaton as Rust code or a binary blob that directly represents the transition table, eliminating runtime construction entirely (as done in one Zig implementation)[\[36\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=stevehanov).

* **Open-source projects:** Beyond Amedee’s fst-gaddag, there are a few other relevant projects. The **Quackle** engine (C++), while not Rust, is open-source and implements a GADDAG for move generation[\[8\]](https://people.csail.mit.edu/jasonkb/quackle/doc/how_quackle_plays_scrabble.html#:~:text=This%20block%20takes%20a%20rack,Faster%20Scrabble%20Move%20Generation%20Algorithm). Studying Quackle’s data structures could inform a Rust translation. On the Rust side, **Andy Kurnia’s** work is noteworthy: the Macondo Scrabble AI (written in Go) uses a *“Kurnia Word Graph (KWG)”*, which is a highly optimized word graph format credited to Andy Kurnia[\[38\]](https://github.com/domino14/macondo#:~:text=Macondo%20interfaces%20with%20it%20as,com). Developers claim the KWG for a 250k word list is only \~5 MB in memory[\[39\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=which%20takes%20around%20100%20MB,in%20memory)[\[40\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=I%20cannot%20follow%20and%20or,it%20is%20true%20and%20how), implying a very efficient compression (possibly even more aggressive sharing than a standard GADDAG). The exact structure isn’t fully documented publicly, but it likely involves similar concepts (alphabet reordering, tail merging, bit-packing, etc.). There’s also a Rust project on GitHub called **gaddag-rust** (by Innoviox) which implemented a GADDAG-based Scrabble AI with a visual simulator. It could be insightful to review its implementation for design patterns (rack handling, board integration, etc.). Finally, Rust crates like [dawg](https://crates.io/crates/dawg) or [rusty-dawg](https://crates.io/crates/rusty-dawg) provide generic DAWG building blocks, though without Scrabble-specific logic. In summary, a combination of these resources can be used to guide the construction of a memory-efficient GADDAG in Rust.

**Design patterns & performance tricks:** A few key patterns emerge from these implementations:

* *Flat memory storage:* Prefer a single contiguous structure (like a vector or array of nodes) over pointers to heap-allocated nodes. This enables using indices (which can be smaller than 64-bit pointers) and improves cache locality[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this). For example, store all nodes in a Vec\<Node\> and refer to children by indices (offsets). Ensure the node struct is compact (e.g., using u32 or even bitfields as shown above).

* *Alphabet encoding:* Use an efficient mapping for letters. Typical Scrabble has 26 letters plus a blank. Many implementations map letters to numeric IDs and sometimes use bit tricks. For instance, one engine represents blank tiles by setting a high-order bit on the letter ID[\[41\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=89,Tile). You can also place the delimiter symbol in the ordering (e.g., use @ or a special char code 0 as the separator, which sorts before A in ASCII)[\[42\]](https://williame.github.io/#:~:text=The%20key%20thing%20is%20that,enough%20in%20the%20graphs%20too). This consistent ordering is important for sorting and merging nodes deterministically.

* *Terminal markers:* Instead of storing a separate child for “end of word” (e.g., a terminal node), some designs use a boolean flag in the node to indicate a word ending[\[43\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=ericlang%20%20April%2021%2C%202025%2C,4%3A14pm%20%2010)[\[44\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Trie%2C%20tree%20whatever%20Image%3A%20%3Aslight_smile%3A,is%20just%20one%20boolean%3A%20is_whole_word). Others, like the example in Will Edwards’ blog, keep terminators as separate child nodes but then optimize by merging them or storing a bitset of multiple word-end flags in one node[\[45\]](https://williame.github.io/#:~:text=The%20first%20thing%20to%20note,B%20and%20C%20in%20it). Minimizing how end-of-word is represented can save a lot of space because every word contributes one end marker.

* *Precomputation vs. on-the-fly:* Building the entire GADDAG upfront (either at compile-time or load-time) is usually acceptable, since it only needs to be done once. Pre-sorting the word list is essential for minimization efficiency[\[29\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=%24%20fst%20set%20,fst). If startup time is a concern, consider distributing the prebuilt automaton (as a file or Rust static byte array) so that the program can directly load it. This is exactly what the fst approach enables (memory-mapping a prebuilt automaton)[\[32\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=static%20dict%3A%20Fst%3A%3ASet%20%3D%20include_bytes%21%28,). The result is that lookups and traversals at runtime are just array indexing operations – extremely fast.

* *Hybrid structures:* One might wonder about integrating a DAWG and GADDAG or using a hybrid. In practice, a **GADDAG is itself stored as a DAWG** (a minimized graph) of the augmented word list. So the hybrid is basically *GADDAG data \+ DAWG compression*. Another possible hybrid is to use separate forward and reverse tries: e.g., have a normal trie for suffixes and a reverse trie for prefixes, and try to coordinate them during search. However, this gets complicated when you have to “meet in the middle” at the anchor letter[\[46\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=%E2%80%9Cwords%20that%20end%20with%20PLAIN%E2%80%9D). The GADDAG effectively encodes that meeting-in-the-middle by its delimiter transition. Given the low memory cost of a compressed GADDAG today, most modern implementations don’t bother with more complex hybrids – they go all-in on the GADDAG. That said, one could explore using a DAWG for the base dictionary and an auxiliary index mapping each letter (or letter+position) to words containing them, but that’s essentially reimplementing the GADDAG functionality in a different form.

## Move Generation and Board Integration

With an efficient GADDAG in place, the next challenge is integrating it with the Scrabble board state to generate moves. **Move generation** entails finding all placements of one or more tiles from the player’s rack that form valid words and connect to existing tiles on the board. The process must obey three constraints: **board constraints** (new tiles must attach to the existing pattern), **rack constraints** (only letters available in the rack can be used, unless using blanks as wildcards), and **dictionary constraints** (all formed sequences must be valid words)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=Any%20move,to%20three%20types%20of%20constraints).

The standard approach, pioneered by Appel & Jacobson and refined by Gordon, is a **one-dimensional search**: iterate over each row (for horizontal plays) and each column (for vertical plays) as the potential word axis, and generate plays in that line considering the existing tiles as fixed markers. Each line has certain **anchor squares** – positions where a new word could potentially start or intersect an existing tile[\[48\]](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15451-s06/www/lectures/scrabble.pdf#:~:text=number%20of%20moves%20available%20at,of%20Selchow%20and%20Richter%20Company)[\[49\]](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15451-s06/www/lectures/scrabble.pdf#:~:text=2.%20COMPUTER%20SCRABBLE,SCRABBLE%20experts%20who%20reviewed%20MONTY). Typically, an empty square adjacent to at least one filled square is an anchor, as is the board’s center for the first move.

**Cross-checks:** A crucial optimization before searching through the dictionary is to precompute **cross-check sets** for empty squares. A cross-check is the set of letters that can be placed in that empty square without violating perpendicular (crossword) validity[\[50\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=As%20players%20make%20moves%20and,checks)[\[51\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Each%20letter%20below%20the%20equals,of%20my%20head%2C%20not%20exhaustive). For example, if an empty square has an T directly above it and an A below (forming a vertical gap), only letters that form valid 3-letter words *T?A* are allowed in that square. Rather than checking this on the fly for every candidate word, we compute for each empty cell the allowed letters by scanning the dictionary of 2-letter and 3-letter words. This set changes only when the letters around that cell change, so it can be cached and updated incrementally each turn[\[50\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=As%20players%20make%20moves%20and,checks)[\[52\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=So%20now%20we%20can%20build,plays%20in%20that%20position%20first). Using cross-checks dramatically prunes the search: the move generator will **“not waste time formulating a word... then checking if the cross-words are valid”**, it will *“formulate only the words that are valid plays in that position”*[\[53\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=list%20is%20off%20the%20top,of%20my%20head%2C%20not%20exhaustive). In practice, each anchor square gets an associated mask or list of allowable letters. If the player doesn’t have any of those letters in their rack (or blanks), there’s no need to consider placing a tile there.

**Generating moves with GADDAG:** Given an anchor and cross-check info, the algorithm does a depth-first search through the GADDAG to build valid words. The procedure can be described in steps (assuming we handle horizontal moves, and analogous for vertical):

1. **Preparation:** Identify the anchor square index on the line (say column j on row i). Let’s call the squares to the left of the anchor (on the same row) positions j-1, j-2, ... and to the right j+1, j+2, .... We also know which of those positions already have letters on the board. We will traverse the GADDAG in sync with placing tiles to the left and right of the anchor.

2. **Initial state:** Start at the GADDAG root (state 0\) with the anchor position as the current focus. We have not placed any new tiles yet. There are two scenarios:

3. **Empty anchor** (normal case): The anchor square is empty and must be filled by one of our rack letters. We will consider each possible rack letter (including blanks as any letter) that is allowed by that anchor’s cross-check set and that leads to a valid transition in the GADDAG.

4. **Occupied anchor** (hook-through case): The anchor corresponds to a letter already on the board (part of an existing word we are extending through). In this case, we *don’t place a tile on the anchor*; instead, we must incorporate the anchor’s letter as a given. We immediately move to the GADDAG child state for that letter (as if that letter were the separator point)[\[54\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=Anchor%20squares%20also%20have%20direction,V%20is%20some%20future%20lexicons). In Gordon’s algorithm, anchor squares also carry a direction, and an occupied anchor is handled by traversing those board letters in the GADDAG before using any rack tiles[\[54\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=Anchor%20squares%20also%20have%20direction,V%20is%20some%20future%20lexicons)[\[55\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=For%20playing%20through%20LOG%2C%20the,the%20GADDAG%20to%20play%20HOLOGRAM). We’ll illustrate this in a moment.

5. **Extend Left (prefix):** From the anchor, we attempt to place letters to the **left** (i.e. in descending column indices) using available rack tiles. In the GADDAG, moving left corresponds to consuming characters *before* the separator. Because the GADDAG stored prefixes in reverse order, each letter we place to the left should follow a valid arc in the automaton from the current state (starting at the anchor’s state). We recursively try all possible letters that:

6. Are present in our remaining rack (or a blank which can represent any needed letter).

7. Appear as a valid transition from the current GADDAG state.

8. Satisfy the cross-check of that left square (if any perpendicular letter constraints there).

We place one letter, advance to the next state in the GADDAG, and move the focus one cell further left. Each placed tile is removed from the rack multiset for the recursion. We continue this until we either run out of rack tiles or reach the board boundary or hit another tile on the board. If we hit a **filled square on the left**, we must stop placing further left (we can’t overwrite it), but we also must ensure the GADDAG path can continue through that letter. In other words, encountering a fixed board letter to the left means: check if the current GADDAG state has a child arc matching that letter; if so, transition into that state and then halt further left-expansion. (At that point, we have effectively included that board letter as part of the prefix.) If no such transition exists, the partial prefix we were building is not compatible with that fixed letter, so this branch of the search fails.

At each left-extension step, we also have the **option to stop extending left** and transition to the right (suffix) side. In the GADDAG, this corresponds to following the delimiter (\+) arc out of the current state (if one exists)[\[56\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=start%20on%20an%20anchor%20square%2C,complete%20words%20along%20the%20way). The presence of a delimiter arc means we have a complete reversed prefix in hand. We typically only take the delimiter when we are ready to start placing to the right (you can imagine this as deciding where the “split” of the word will occur relative to the anchor). The algorithm as described by Gordon says: *“at each step \[moving leftward\], look for the delimiter in the arcs, go on the arc for the delimiter, and start moving rightward...”*[\[57\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=start%20on%20an%20anchor%20square%2C,complete%20words%20along%20the%20way). In practice, an implementation might do this: every time you place a letter or encounter a stop condition on the left, you attempt to take the \+ transition as one possible move (which then switches to the right expansion phase described next).

1. **Extend Right (suffix):** Once the delimiter has been taken (implicitly or explicitly), we begin filling to the **right** of the original anchor. Now we proceed in increasing column indices from the anchor. The GADDAG state we carry forward already encodes whatever prefix (if any) we built. From this point, the search is similar to a standard trie traversal to build the suffix:

2. If we encounter a board letter on the next right square, we must match it. Check if the current automaton state has a child for that letter; if not, this path fails (the word we’re forming isn’t in the dictionary when extended by that board letter). If it does, advance into that state and move further right. Critically, since we didn’t use a rack tile for this (the letter is already on the board), our rack contents remain the same. We *do* need to ensure the perpendicular cross formed by this existing letter and any new tiles we place is still valid, but existing letters were already on the board from previous turns, so they should have had valid crosses at placement time. (We still check any new perpendicular words formed by *new* tiles as a final verification step.)

3. If the next right square is empty, we consider placing a tile from the rack. Similar to the left side, we iterate over rack letters that are available and allowed by that square’s cross-check set. For each such letter that has a corresponding child arc from the current state, we place it and consume the tile, then continue right. If a square is empty but we have no rack letter that produces a valid continuation in the GADDAG, that branch is a dead end.

4. We terminate the rightward expansion when we either reach a square beyond the board or a filled square that ended our word. At that point, if the current state in the GADDAG is marked as a terminal (i.e., we have a complete word)[\[44\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Trie%2C%20tree%20whatever%20Image%3A%20%3Aslight_smile%3A,is%20just%20one%20boolean%3A%20is_whole_word), we have found a valid play. We record the assembled word and its placement (and we would compute its score based on Scrabble scoring rules). If the state is not terminal, it means the letters we placed form only a prefix of some dictionary word, not a full word, so that placement is invalid unless the word continues to another existing tile (the check for which would have kept us going).

5. **Backtracking:** The algorithm explores all combinations by backtracking – removing placed tiles and trying different letters or different split points. Thanks to the GADDAG, this search is pruned heavily by the dictionary: we only follow paths that lead to actual words. Any attempt to put a letter that doesn’t lead to a real word is cut off immediately by a missing arc in the automaton. The cross-checks further cut off any move that would create an illegal short cross-word. The result is a very efficient enumeration of legal moves.

To illustrate this with a **concrete example**, consider a board situation with the word “LOG” already on the board (occupying, say, columns 5-7 of our row) and suppose we have the letters to form “HOLOGRAM”. How does the generator find “HOLOGRAM”? According to Gordon: *“the anchor square would be the L \[of LOG\] and the algorithm would have to traverse the L, O and G through the GADDAG before trying to play any tiles on the rack”*[\[55\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=For%20playing%20through%20LOG%2C%20the,the%20GADDAG%20to%20play%20HOLOGRAM). In other words, we treat the letter L (column 5\) as the hook point (anchor). The algorithm starts at L (which is filled, so no tile placed) and moves left: it can place H then O to the left of L (forming “HOL” to the left, reversed as “LOH” in the GADDAG path). It will stop extending left either because we decide that’s enough or because we hit the border before that. Let’s say it stops after placing “HO” to the left. It then takes the delimiter and switches to extending right. Now it incorporates the O and G already on the board to the right of L – the GADDAG state will expect those letters in sequence, and it should succeed because “HOLOG” is a prefix of a word in the dictionary (we are essentially following the path HO \+ LOG in the GADDAG). After the G, the next board square is empty, so it places R, then A, then M, each matching the next required letter in the GADDAG path “HOLOGRAM”. When it reaches the end of “HOLOGRAM” in the automaton (a terminal state) and also has no more letters to place (we used all 5 from “HO” \+ “RAM” from the rack, assuming we had blanks or the exact letters needed), it records that as a valid move. Notice how the existing “LOG” was seamlessly integrated: the algorithm never tried to form a word that overwrote or ignored those letters (like “HAPPYLOG” nonsense) because the GADDAG traversal required matching them exactly[\[58\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=understand%20it%2C%20the%20square%20before,What%20am%20I%20getting%20wrong)[\[55\]](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53938369/how-to-check-if-a-letter-is-allowed-on-a-square-in-the-gaddag-move-generation#:~:text=For%20playing%20through%20LOG%2C%20the,the%20GADDAG%20to%20play%20HOLOGRAM).

**Blank tiles:** Blanks (wildcards) add another wrinkle. Typically, blanks are handled by iterating through all possible letter assignments for the blank at the point of placement. For example, if we have a blank in the rack and we want to try placing it in a position, we loop letter from A to Z and if the GADDAG has an arc for that letter, we treat it as a valid transition (and mark that we used a blank). The GADDAG itself can remain unaware of blanks – it’s purely matching letters. We just allow a blank tile to satisfy any required letter. In move generation code, this is often done by branching: if tile X is a blank, try every letter that is in the child list of the current node. It’s important to carry the information that a blank was used (for scoring and output, blanks have no score and need a special notation to differentiate from actual letters). Some engines encode blanks in the GADDAG by treating blank as a special character, but it’s simpler to handle it in the search logic (e.g., treat blank on the rack as a wildcard that can take the place of any needed letter).

**Move validation and scoring:** Each generated move needs to be validated for cross-words and then scored. The cross-checks we applied ensure that any new letter we placed had a valid perpendicular word. However, when multiple new tiles are placed, we should verify that the perpendicular words formed at *each* new tile are valid. In practice, because we only ever placed letters that satisfied the cross-check at that square, those perpendicular words are guaranteed to be valid dictionary words of length 2 or more. We also must ensure at least one new tile was placed (Scrabble rules require using at least one tile from your rack; our algorithm inherently does this because it only generates plays with rack letters). Scoring involves summing letter values with board multipliers, including 50-point bonus for using all 7 tiles (which the generator can flag when rack usage \== 7). These are outside the scope of the data structure but need to be integrated into the move generation output.

In summary, **the integration of the GADDAG with board state** is what makes exhaustive move generation feasible. The GADDAG provides *fast lexicon lookup in both directions*, while the board provides positional constraints and hook letters. Techniques like cross-check pruning and carefully ordered DFS (placing left parts first, then right) ensure that only legal plays are explored[\[53\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=list%20is%20off%20the%20top,of%20my%20head%2C%20not%20exhaustive). The result is that even with thousands of possible combinations of letters, a modern GADDAG-based move generator can enumerate all moves on a Scrabble board in a fraction of a second on current hardware. In fact, with an optimized GADDAG, **move generation is no longer the bottleneck** – the AI’s decision-making (evaluating and simulating moves) usually dominates runtime[\[59\]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HP90knHlYqc#:~:text=Wacky%20History%20of%20Computer%20Scrabble,Either%20is%20considered%20acceptable).

## Conclusion

For the *TileTangle* project (a Scrabble-like game in Rust), leveraging a GADDAG data structure is a wise choice to achieve fast move generation. Key resources to draw on include Steven Gordon’s original paper for the algorithmic foundation[\[4\]](https://hana-sebia.github.io/uploads/faster-scrabble-gordon.pdf#:~:text=the%20trie%20of%20a%20large,moves%20more%20than%20twice%20as)[\[60\]](https://hana-sebia.github.io/uploads/faster-scrabble-gordon.pdf#:~:text=large%20lexicon,For%20a), the community blog posts dissecting GADDAG and cross-check implementation[\[61\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=The%20first%20idea%20,our%20options%20would%20be%20AXE)[\[62\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=list%20is%20off%20the%20top,of%20my%20head%2C%20not%20exhaustive), and existing Rust implementations like Amedee d'Aboville’s *fst-gaddag* for concrete code examples[\[35\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=There%20we%20have%20it%2C%20the,blocks%20for%20a%20Scrabble%20AI). By constructing a minimized bidirectional word graph (either via Rust’s fst or a custom trie), using memory-efficient node representations[\[23\]](https://ziggit.dev/t/gaddag-optimization/7343#:~:text=Using%20standard%20pointers%20will%20bloat,lots%20of%20clues%20about%20this), and integrating cross-check tables and anchor-scanning logic, one can create a Scrabble move generator that is both **high-performance** and **comprehensive**. The GADDAG’s ability to handle partial word expansions from any anchor point, combined with Rust’s low-level control over memory, will allow *TileTangle* to generate moves with the speed needed for AI play without sacrificing correctness. All the techniques discussed – from bit-packed trie nodes to cached cross sets – contribute to an engine that can play Scrabble at an expert level, exploring thousands of moves within milliseconds and doing so in a memory-efficient manner[\[31\]](https://amedee.me/2020/11/04/fst-gaddag/#:~:text=Scrabble%20AI%2C%20and%20this%20significantly,so%20it%E2%80%99s%20worth%20the%20tradeoff)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GADDAG#:~:text=moves%20require%20words%20that%20,1).
